name: Stone massage

card.summary: A massage using heated smooth stones placed on or moved over the body, used to relax muscles and calm the body, supporting a rested, less tense look.
card.note: Hot stones can burn skin; several medical conditions are contraindications.

quick.overview:
Stone massage uses smooth heated stones, usually basalt, placed on the body or held by the therapist while massaging. It is a spa treatment aimed at relaxation and eased muscle tension.

For looks, the chain is indirect: relaxation, sleep and muscle ease can contribute to a rested, less tense appearance. Trials in orthopedic surgery patients found lower postoperative pain, anxiety and better sleep with hot stone massage than routine care.[2][3][4]
quick.how: Stones are heated in water, typically to about 38 to 60 degrees C, and used for 60 to 90 minute sessions, often combined with Swedish or deep tissue massage.[1]
quick.risks: Hot stones on bare skin can burn, and people under the influence of drugs or alcohol may misjudge temperature. Diabetes, epilepsy, heart disease, neuropathy, certain skin conditions, broken skin and varicose veins are listed as contraindications.[1]

lead: Stone massage, or hot stone massage, is a treatment in which heated stones are placed on the body or used by the therapist to apply pressure. Basalt is most common. Wikipedia reports similar traditions in many cultures, and American therapist Mary D. Nelson developed LaStone Therapy in 1993.[1]

People use it for relaxation and muscle ease, which supports a rested look and skin warmth rather than a structural change. A thermography study in 40 healthy men found surface temperature rises in the trunk and shoulder girdle after hot stone massage.[5]

chain: Muscle tension, stress and pain eased
Rested, less tense look and warmer skin
angle.text: The look-related payoff comes through relaxation, sleep and muscle ease rather than reshaping anything. The warmth also raises surface skin temperature during and after treatment.

paras: Therapists heat volcanic stones, set them on a towel as a buffer, place them along the body or hold them to press into muscles. Some use salt stones, wax or electric dry-heat units, which carry extra safety concerns.[1] Practitioners cite circulation, sleep, flexibility and stress benefits; reviews describe weak short-term benefits for massage in general and limited stone-specific research.[1]
Burns are the main hazard, and contraindications include diabetes, epilepsy, heart disease and neuropathy.[1]

A 99-patient randomized trial after orthopedic surgery found hot stone and slow-stroke back massage each lowered pain versus routine care (adjusted mean difference about -2.5 on a visual analog scale).[2] The same cohort showed lower anxiety[3] and the sleep study compared the two massages with routine care.[4] A thermovision study of 40 men found temperature rises after hot stone massage in the back of the trunk and shoulder girdle.[5]

timeline.event: Mary D. Nelson develops LaStone Therapy.[1]
